answer:
**An offline ranking gain is evidence about a measured dataset, not a guarantee of product improvement.** NDCG evaluates ordering under particular relevance labels and candidate sets. Production additionally includes latency, exposure, freshness, downstream business logic, and users reacting to what they see. [1](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml)

**Seven distinct diagnoses are worth separating.** Train–serve skew can change feature values. Higher latency can cause timeouts or abandonment. Historical position/selection bias can make offline labels favor the old exposure policy. Reduced exploration or diversity can improve short-term fit while worsening satisfaction. Miscalibrated probabilities can break auction/value calculations even with better ranking. Stale embeddings can make serving candidates differ from evaluation. Feedback loops or cannibalization can shift activity rather than create additional value.

**Investigate in causal order.** Verify assignment and logging first. Compare actual serving inputs/outputs with offline replay. Inspect timeouts and tail latency, then slice candidate recall, calibration, and user outcomes. Confirm that the supposedly improved model version and compatible index were actually served.

An aggregate 1.2% decline may come from one high-value cohort or one device path. Examine those slices with appropriate uncertainty and multiplicity awareness rather than searching until a convenient story appears.

Rollback if prespecified guardrails fail while preserving diagnostic logs. The repair should address the observed mechanism: more offline tuning will not fix a client timeout, and a faster server will not fix biased relevance labels.

**Technical details and references.**

Seven distinct causes are training/serving feature skew, extra latency/timeouts, position-biased historical labels, reduced diversity/exploration, miscalibrated probabilities breaking downstream decisions, stale retrieval/embedding state, and feedback or cannibalization effects that offline ranking metrics omit. [1](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml) [2](https://research.google/pubs/the-ml-test-score-a-rubric-for-ml-production-readiness-and-technical-debt-reduction/)

First verify randomization and logging, then compare online/offline feature values and replay the same requests through both paths. Decompose effects by latency, user/item cohort, candidate source, and downstream decision. NDCG rewards relevance ordering on the labeled list; it does not directly encode revenue, retention, or system failures.

Use shadow traffic to test execution parity, followed by a bounded randomized rollout with guardrails. Do not change multiple components simultaneously during diagnosis. A positive offline delta is evidence worth testing, not authorization to ignore a negative causal online result.
